Nach ihrem Jubiläum im vergangenen Jahr begrüßt die Bucerius Summer School ihre Teilnehmenden vom 7. bis 17. August 2026 mit einem neuen Motto: „Skills, Scenarios, Leadership“ ist nun nicht nur Teil des Logos des Fortbildungs- und Netzwerk-Events, sondern bringt auch die entsprechende inhaltliche Justierung mit sich. So nimmt der Vorsatz, Handlungsfähigkeit unter jungen Führungskräften auf globaler Ebene zu stärken, einen präsenten Teil in der Programmgestaltung ein. Ziel des in Kooperation mit der Karl Schlecht Stiftung realisierten Seminars bleibt dabei weiterhin, Führungsqualitäten zu fördern, indem junge Fachkräfte in einen internationalen Dialog über aktuelle politische, wirtschaftliche, soziale und rechtliche Fragen eingebunden werden. Die Teilnehmenden lernen von bekannten Referent;innen und Persönlichkeiten aus Politik, Wirtschaft, Wissenschaft und dem NGO-Bereich. Im Kontext der Szenario-Entwicklung schauen die Teilnehmenden auf konkrete Entwicklungen und Herausforderungen für die Zukunft und diskutieren über ihre Perspektiven zur Stärkung von Demokratie und internationalem Zusammenhalt.

Seminarprogramm mit hochkarätigen Talks für Teilnehmende aus 27 Nationen

An dem 10-tägigen Programm nehmen in diesem Jahr 53 Führungskräfte im Alter von 28 bis 36 Jahren aus insgesamt 27 Nationen teil. Nominiert wurden sie von Regierungschefs, Minister:innen, Unternehmensvorständ:innen, Universitäten, Medienhäusern und Direktionen internationaler Organisationen. Gemeinsam mit dem Projektteam des Bereichs Politik & Gesellschaft der ZEIT STIFTUNG BUCERIUS reisen die Teilnehmenden im Rahmen des Programms nach Hamburg, Lübeck und Berlin. Vor allem in der Hauptstadt stehen Besuche mit hochkarätigen Regierungsvertreter:innen auf dem Plan, unter anderem im Bundeskanzleramt, beim Auswärtigen Amt und dem Verteidigungsministerium. Die Teilnehmenden besuchen außerdem die Hertie School, das ANCB The Aedes Metropolitan Laboratory auf dem Campus des  Aedes Architekturforums und nehmen an einem Workshop des Auschwitz Institute for the Prevention of Genocide and Mass Atrocities teil. Weiteres Kulturprogramm erwartet die Gruppe in Hamburg beim Internationalen Sommerfestival auf Kampnagel oder in Lübeck bei einem Besuch des Europäischen Hansemuseums.

Kriege, KI und Desinformationen: Welche Herausforderungen das Programm noch in den Blick nimmt

Der Hauptteil des Programms findet in Hamburg statt und schaut auf internationale gesellschaftliche und politische Fragen, die in Talks, Keynotes, immersiven Workshops und Simulationen diskutiert werden. Zu den Themen gehören unter anderem der Einfluss der zweiten Präsidentschaft von Donald Trump und die US-amerikanische Außenpolitik im Krieg mit dem Iran, die Einwirkungen von Künstlicher Intelligenz auf politische Regelwerke sowie Entwicklungen in der Mobilität, Pressefreiheit im Zeitalter von Desinformationen und Selbstführung in einer sich rasant weiterentwickelnden Welt.

Die Bucerius Summer School wird von uns als ZEIT STIFTUNG BUCERIUS seit über 25 Jahren in Anlehnung an die berühmte internationale Summer School der Harvard University in den USA realisiert. In den 1960er-Jahren kamen dort aufstrebende Führungskräfte aus aller Welt zu Debatten und Vorträgen zusammen. Viele der Absolvent:innen des Seminars wurden später Minister:innen, Wissenschaftler:innen oder prominente Journalist:innen – führende Persönlichkeiten in ihren jeweiligen Fachgebieten.

Mehr zur Bucerius Summer School hier.

Viele Perspektiven von Menschen der Hamburger Stadtgesellschaft finden sich im Museum für Hamburgische Geschichte (MHG) bislang nicht wieder. Während der derzeit stattfindenden baulichen und inhaltlichen Modernisierung lädt das MHG Menschen dazu ein, ihre Geschichten zu erzählen und Lebenswirklichkeiten zu teilen, damit einige davon langfristig Eingang in die Sammlungen und Ausstellungen finden können.

Mithilfe von Beteiligungsformaten – ob digitale Formate oder Treffpunkte an öffentlichen Orten in den verschiedenen Stadtteilen – möchten wir Hamburger:innen ermutigen, ihre Lebenswirklichkeiten zu teilen.

Wir laden Dich ein, auch Deine Geschichte mit uns zu teilen. Ob kurz, lang, ernst oder humorvoll – alles ist willkommen. Was verbindet dich mit Hamburg? Wo fühlst du dich zu Hause? Wann hast du Zugehörigkeit oder Ausgrenzung erlebt? Was soll so bleiben, wie es ist – was möchtest du verändern? Teile gerne etwas über Dein Leben und Deinen Alltag in der Stadt oder in Deinem Stadtteil, Deine Wünsche und Hoffnungen für Hamburg.

  • Aktuell
  • Komm vorbei!
  • Programmübersicht
  • Kontakt

Aktuell

Mein Hamburg! im KörberHaus in Bergedorf

Auftaktabend am 06.08.2026 um 18:30 Uhr

Das Museum für Hamburgische Geschichte ist vom 04.08. bis 22.08. zu Besuch im KörberHaus in Bergedorf. Wir laden dich ein, deine Geschichte zu teilen.

Zu viele Perspektiven der Menschen unserer Stadt kommen im Museum nicht vor. Das wollen wir gemeinsam ändern! Mein Hamburg kommt zu dir nach Bergedorf!

Zum Auftakt am Donnerstag, den 6. August 2026, erwartet dich ab 18:30 Uhr ein vielseitiger Abend zwischen Lesung, Erzählung und Live-Musik von Bergedorfer Künstler:innen, der die Besonderheiten des Stadtteils hörbar, sichtbar und erlebbar macht.

With the development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), online violence against journalists has taken a new turn. The online environment was already unsafe for journalists, but now AI acts as a catalyst for online harassment, intimidation, and subversion. AI facilitates existing forms of online violence against journalists, such as identity fraud, threats, and sexual violence. That is why we refer to “AI-facilitated violence” in this article. This includes so-called deepfakes: AI-generated videos, photos, or audio clips that are difficult to distinguish from real footage. One primary form of AI use is the so-called AI-facilitated “scam.” In this scenario, the journalist’s reputation or expertise is exploited to promote a scam. Seventeen of the 58 incidents investigated fall into this category. This development undermines the credibility and expertise of journalists. In the fintech sector, where new technology is being developed for the financial world, deepfake scams rose by 700% in 2023.

One example is the case of Gabriel Mellqvist, a Swedish journalist who covers financial news. An AI-generated fake advertisement for an investment platform pretended that he was endorsing it. As a result, approximately 500 investors were defrauded, with a total loss of about 500 million Swedish kronor (approximately 46 million euros). The journalist himself says he is frustrated that his reputation has been damaged by this incident.

A second category consists of Russian disinformation campaigns. These campaigns use personas of journalists (and sometimes entire news websites) to spread pro-Russian or anti-Ukrainian narratives. They do not produce original content but re-post information from pro-Russian social media accounts and news channels to reach a Western audience. In addition, Storm 15-16, Matryoshka, and Doppelganger are characterized as “information laundering.” This means that disinformation is posted and disseminated on a massive scale, in part thanks to AI, so that its origin becomes unrecognizable. 

Since July 2023, more than 8 million fake articles have been re-posted by the Pravda Network, according to the monitoring website portal-kombat.com, an initiative of the fact-checking organization Checkfirst. In addition, Matryoshka is particularly known for spreading AI deepfakes. Doppelganger mimics official news websites, sometimes using AI-generated content. Behind these websites are organizations funded by the Russian government.

A third category consists of sexual deepfakes. In these cases, AI is used to generate sexual images of journalists without their consent. Five of the 58 analyzed incidents fall into this category. Deepfakes are increasing rapidly. In 2023, there were an estimated 500,000 deepfakes online; according to a forecast, this number rose to 8 million by 2025. As many as 96–98% of all deepfakes consist of non-consensual sexual content online, with women being the victims in 99% of cases. For example, previous research has shown that women may withdraw from the public sphere or be unable to continue practicing their profession.

The psychological harm suffered by victims can be comparable to that caused by physical sexual violence. Furthermore, AI-generated images are difficult to remove from the internet. 2. Use tools to identify and expose disinformation

3. Continue to report incidents to:

1. Monitoring organizations such as the MFRR

2. Relevant legal authorities (see an overview of the most important ones in Europe here)

3. Organizations that provide support for online abuse and violence, such as Offlimits.

One primary form of AI use is the so-called AI-facilitated “scam.” In this scenario, the journalist’s reputation or expertise is exploited to promote a scam. In the fintech sector, where new technology is being developed for the financial world, deepfake scams rose by 700% in 2023.

One example is the case of Gabriel Mellqvist, a Swedish journalist who covers financial news. An AI-generated fake advertisement for an investment platform pretended that he was endorsing it. As a result, approximately 500 investors were defrauded, with a total loss of about 500 million Swedish kronor (approximately 46 million euros). The journalist himself says he is frustrated that his reputation has been damaged by this incident.

AI-powered disinformation — effects on democracy in Africa

Karen Allen, Senior Research Associate at Institute for Security Studies (ISS) in South Africa and a former BBC foreign correspondent, examines how AI is being weaponized to spread disinformation across Africa.

AI-assisted fact-checking in Arabic: the Kashif chatbot

The fact-checking organisation Kashif operates out of Ramallah in the West Bank. In this video, founder Riham Abu Aita explains how the Kashif bot, an Arabic-language chatbot that supports user queries, was developed and implemented.

Christo Buschek: Unraveling the AI black box

Algorithmic systems such as AI are taking hold in our societies and daily lives. Yet, the inner workings of these systems are opaque and often kept secret.

Nikita Roy: How conversational AI is changing journalism

The founder of Newsroom Robots Lab at Harvard breaks down how conversational AI is revolutionizing journalism.

items.content_html:
I am a female Afghan photographer who never accepted photography as a normal profession. For me, photography is a lofty goal, a golden opportunity, a window of hope for tomorrow and a means of communication between me and the people beyond the borders of Afghanistan. For me, photography is like an unfinished story, each page of which depicts a bitter event, an unforgivable history, an unjust document, and frequent anomalies of a patriarchal land like Afghanistan.

I photograph in a land where my fellow citizens are pushed to the margins more than yesterday and are further and further away from their basic social, cultural and artistic rights. I have not chosen photography only as a source of income, but to narrate the inhuman events against the deprived women of my land. 

Photography becomes meaningful for me when I have been able to depict the standing, courage and justice of women with the re-domination of the Taliban in Afghanistan. 

I chose to be a photographer. Photography becomes meaningful for me when I have been able to depict the standing, courage and justice of women with the re-domination of the Taliban in Afghanistan. This period of suffocation and injustice cast a shadow on the lives of Afghan women. The Taliban took away the right to education, work and all freedoms from women and girls. That is, they removed women from the society as a whole.  

In the misogynistic and patriarchal society of the Taliban, women have no rights. But this limitation cannot stop me and other strong and brave Afghan women from working and progressing. Women will not go back, they have worked hard for 20 years to be seen and heard, they are aware of their rights and have understood how to live freely.  

As a professional female photographer who lives in Afghanistan and with the restrictions that the men of the family have on women, only I, as an Afghan female photographer, can photograph them and I must try to show my values and the women of the society. 

How do brave Afghan women and girls resist and fight against Taliban and bypass restrictions? With photography, I can depict challenges faced by women and their struggle and tell an illustrated history of Afghan women's resistance stories.  

I believe that every story I tell will make a difference in someone's life.

items.content_html:
Culture is

We face a scenario in which groups marginalised from global society continue to seek their own spaces from which they can contradict stereotypes, resist the labelling gaze of colonisers, and, on the other side of the coin, plant dreams, water the land, and foster growth in a forest of life.

A story by Djamila RIBEIRO

I’m making a song
where my mother and all mothers
will see themselves mirrored,
a song that speaks like two eyes

I’m walking on a road
that runs through many countries.
They may not see me, but I see
and salute my friends.
(…)
My life, our lives,
form a single diamond.
I’ve learned new words
and made others more beautiful.

I’m making a song
for waking up men
and putting children to sleep.

"Friendly Song" poem by Carlos Drummond de Andrade, song by Milton Nascimento. 

We face a scenario in which groups marginalised from global society continue to seek their own spaces from which they can contradict stereotypes, resist the labelling gaze of colonisers, and, on the other side of the coin, plant dreams, water the land, and foster growth in a forest of life. We often come across gazes which focus on these groups in isolation from each other, as if they were disconnected from a dialectical relationship to imperialism. At the end of the day, as Tejumola Olaniyan (1959–2019) taught us, thinking about Europe as modern in its institutions and development against Africa as a space without modernity ignores the fact that both exist in the same historical time and that the modernity of one was based on the colonisation and exploitation of the other. This idea was important to him because it allowed him to rethink modernity from a global perspective as a shared patrimony.  

At the end of the day, as Tejumola Olaniyan (1959–2019) taught us, thinking about Europe as modern in its institutions and development against Africa as a space without modernity ignores the fact that both exist in the same historical time and that the modernity of one was based on the colonisation and exploitation of the other. 

From birth our bodies are caught in a web of meanings which are out of our control. Regardless of our personal desire for transformation, we are inserted into a system which was operating well before we were born and whose structure remains rooted in the oppression of some groups by others. That is part of our reality, so it can never be an invitation to inaction. As long as we are alive, we can generate energy to sustain the structures of resistance which the oldest of our nonconformists built from their diverse identities and points of view as the grounds upon which modernity was raised. In this sense, a prize like the one given by the Prince Claus Fund will not resolve centuries of discrimination, but it surely will play its part in drawing together an international struggle for humanity. 

An example will help clarify a number of questions. Lélia Gonzalez (1935-94) was a Brazilian social scientist and celebrated precursor of black feminist thought about the country from which I write. As a public intellectual during the period of military dictatorships that raged across South America in the sixties, seventies, and eighties, Gonzalez had no time to waste. She wrote, organised conferences, taught classes to the general public, and participated in debates to show that she was part of the social group most impacted by misery with the hope of somehow altering the balance of forces. 

In her writings from the 1980s, Lélia anticipated the need for a transnational feminist movement when she proposed an ‘Amerafrican’ identity, an identity for the people of the Americas and the Caribbean. This is an edited version of the article by Dale Berning Sawa, originally published on theguardian.com and in Guardian Saturday magazine, under the headline, "South African photographer Zanele Muholi: ‘My mother worked for a white family. I remember the pools I wasn’t allowed to swim in’". You can read the original article here. Courtesy of Guardian News & Media Ltd.

South African visual activist and 2013 Prince Claus Awardee Zanele Muholi has spent nearly three decades changing the face of African art. Working for and with Black LGBTQIA+ communities, their photography affirms dignity, beauty and belonging.

Born in one of the bloodiest moments of apartheid, Muholi’s early life continues to shape their work. Where lazy or unthinking descriptions will often land on “poor” to qualify a background such as Muholi’s, the artist purposefully chooses “under-resourced” instead, underscoring the systemic inequalities at work. They also emphasise what they have gained at every stage: a DIY urgency – a sense of responsibility – to keep making work, driven by the certitude that it really can change lives.

As a child Muholi was cared for by aunties and neighbours, and the wider township community. This sense of belonging to a chosen family is itself expanded throughout their work. In Faces and Phases, their long-running portrait series documenting professionals and experts who play crucial roles in the queer community.

“I always ask people to look good,” they say, “because most images that were done previously by visual anthropologists, they really distorted Africa. You often find that the photographer’s name is there but the person being photographed, their name is not there. I’m trying to fix that and make sure that we are done beautifully in the most amazing way.”

In 2007, Muholi shot a series of portraits of Miss D’Vine, a dancer who worked in the gay bars and drag houses of Johannesburg. Shooting outdoors, using the landscape, was about “undoing the closet” and allowing the subject to be seen. In one image, the dancer wears a beaded isigege, a Zulu maiden’s skirt traditionally worn by young girls during the Reed Dance, when they dance for the Zulu king. “Trans people have not been able to be part of those ceremonies because they are either pre-op, and therefore they don’t qualify, or if they do go there, they might be seen as something else that they do not connect with.”

In Somnyama Ngonyama, a series of self-portraits largely inspired by Muholi’s mother, the artist poses in bold attire: a headdress of a dozen combs or two-dozen wooden clothes pegs; a headwrap and neckpiece made of deflated bike tires. The images questions conventions of beauty and fashion:

“What is beauty to you might not be the same to the next person. What is fashion in the west might be ritual to us, or part of the culture and traditions of the Bantu people.”

The series’ title means “Hail the Dark Lioness” in isiZulu. This is political, as photography is often held to be a western thing. “But when we think, when we plan, when we produce, when we play our music, it is in Zulu – or whatever your native language is.”

Recently recognised with the 2026 Hasselblad Award, Muholi has said the honour is for “all of us, the queer and trans community in Africa” — a recognition carried collectively rather than individually.

Wadi El Qamar, also known as Moon Valley, is a residential area located in the west of Alexandria, Egypt next to the Portland Cement factory. Just ten meters away from the residential area, the factory processes coal and garbage. It layers the homes of more than 30,000 people with toxic dust, causing tremendous health problems to those who live there.

A story by Mohamed MAHDY

Moon Dust

Wadi El Qamar, also known as Moon Valley, is a residential area located in the west of Alexandria, Egypt next to the Portland Cement factory. Just ten meters away from the residential area, the factory processes coal and garbage. It layers the homes of more than 30,000 people with toxic dust, causing tremendous health problems to those who live there.

The Moon Valley is home to 60,000 people, and historical documents show that the residential area was founded more than 70 years ago under King Farouk, predating the cement factory. Residents face enormous incidents of asthma, lung cancer, eye, ear, and throat infections, and chest sensitivities. The health problems caused by the factory dust affect working-age men who cannot support their families due to their deteriorating health conditions. Children are debilitated by these diseases, and the elderly are also particularly at risk. 
 
People there are not living as humanity should. Children are born with asthma. Cement, coal, and car exhaust fills their homes. Every five minutes a new layer of dust appears.  

Mohammed Mahdy has been documenting this project from 2016 to 2020, recording the impacts of this dust on the residents of Moon Valley, and how people are trying to survive. Previous efforts to pressure the cement company had failed, but after Mahdy’s project was exhibited in Cairo, and later featured in the New York Times, national and international attention brought results. The company installed filters to limit their pollution and the health minister promised help with medical costs for the worst affected. 

The story was created and published as part of the Arab Documentary Photography Programme.

The Moon Valley is home to 60,000 people, and historical documents show that the residential area was founded more than 70 years ago under King Farouk, predating the cement factory. Residents face enormous incidents of asthma, lung cancer, eye, ear, and throat infections, and chest sensitivities. The health problems caused by the factory dust affect working-age men who cannot support their families due to their deteriorating health conditions. Children are debilitated by these diseases, and the elderly are also particularly at risk. 
 
People there are not living as humanity should. Children are born with asthma. Cement, coal, and car exhaust fills their homes. Every five minutes a new layer of dust appears.  

Mohammed Mahdy has been documenting this project from 2016 to 2020, recording the impacts of this dust on the residents of Moon Valley, and how people are trying to survive. Previous efforts to pressure the cement company had failed, but after Mahdy’s project was exhibited in Cairo, and later featured in the New York Times, national and international attention brought results. The company installed filters to limit their pollution and the health minister promised help with medical costs for the worst affected. 

The story was created and published as part of the Arab Documentary Photography Programme.

July 11, 2024, is the third anniversary of the historic mass protest in Cuba in which thousands of citizens took to the streets to demand liberty. It is also the third anniversary of Cuban artist and 2022 Prince Claus Impact Awardee Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s imprisonment. He was arrested on his way to the protest, detained for nearly a year, and then sentenced to years of imprisonment for allegedly having insulted the Cuban flag in a performance in 2019, obstruction of justice and disrespect for authority. Since then, he has been in a maximum-security prison surrounded by men serving life sentences for murder. His two requests for a “conditional release” that would allow him to serve the rest of his sentence under house arrest have been rejected by Cuban authorities.

Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara spends his days drawing in the cell that he shares with two other men. He is allowed to draw, but his artworks cannot be taken out of prison to be exhibited. He is not required to work, but he is not allowed to socialize with other prisoners during the daily hour of outdoor exercise. He can speak to friends by phone twice weekly but only one close relative is permitted to visit him in person.

To highlight the third anniversary of Luis's imprisonment we are republishing the article published on Hyperallergic on November 7, 2023 highlighting the anniversary of the Cuban government’s assault on the San Isidro Movement headquarters on November 26, 2020. Luis Otero Alcántara has issued a public statement from prison, delivered by phone and transcribed by his friends.

This text was originally translated, published and updated by Luis's friend and colleague, Coco Fusco, a Cuban-American interdisciplinary artist, writer, and curator.

Cuban Artist’s Message of Defiance From Prison

In 2011, I cast off the shackles of fear and staged my first exhibition “Our Heroes Are Neither Valued nor Respected,” which was inspired by the veterans of the war in Angola. This was my first political manifesto and the starting point of my attempt to usher in change in Cuba, a society paralyzed by fear, apathy, a lack of hope, in which people do not have the power to decide their future. 

On the road that I have traveled since, I have been joined by beings of light, friends with limited economic resources, terminal illnesses, people being cared for by siblings, people with young children, people with differing poetics, people from different social strata and faiths, but all rich in artistic resources. All are full of love for others, and united by their love of freedom. From these exchanges emerged the plan to create an independent #00Biennial, for which we drew on the preceding experiences that the legendary group Omni Zona Franca had with their annual poetry festivals and other endeavors. We organized dozens of concerts and exhibitions. We galvanized a collective movement against Decree 349, the 2018 law that criminalized independent artistic activity that was not authorized by the state. This movement succeeded in politicizing the entire Cuban arts sector, giving rise to more collective action. The San Isidro Movement emerged, and then Hunger Strikers of San Isidro barricaded themselves into the San Isidro headquarters. The Cuban government’s break-in and the arrest of our members, which was documented live on social media, produced an unprecedented public gathering in protest of state power: more than 400 young people carried out a sit-in outside the Ministry of Culture to demand all kinds of freedoms that our people have been denied for so long. More movements and campaigns emerged, such as “Express Yourself,” calling on Cubans to assert their human right to freedom of expression. The San Isidro Movement’s continued protests and hunger strikes forced the rusty wheels of Cuban civil society to begin to turn again. And on Sunday, July 11, 2021, tens of thousands of Cubans took to the streets to demand democracy.

At present, we are beings living in limbo without legal rights, with harsher sentences in many cases than those given to murderers, without options or benefits such as parole, despite our disciplined behavior. While we have been imprisoned, we have lost wives, husbands, and family members. We have missed celebrations, births, watching our children grow. We miss our friends…

2023 is coming to an end. More than two years have passed since the 11th of July 2021. There are more than a thousand political prisoners that have been in prison ever since that great day, including myself. At present, we are beings living in limbo without legal rights, with harsher sentences in many cases than those given to murderers, without options or benefits such as parole, despite our disciplined behavior. While we have been imprisoned, we have lost wives, husbands, and family members. We have missed celebrations, births, watching our children grow. We miss our friends…

In the past year, international figures that allegedly support human rights visited Cuba, but none of them have been able to change our situation. So, I wonder, after shaking President Miguel Díaz-Canel’s hand, did they ask about us? Will we have to wait another four or five years for another UN General Assembly to demand that Cuba respect our human rights? The top leaders of the European Union have visited Havana, but even this highly significant economic partner failed to move the regime so that the political prisoners would not spend another day without embracing their loved ones in freedom, rather than under the watchful eye of a prison guard. 

Some leaders appear not to care about our plight. The president of Mexico and the vice president of Colombia do not recognize the racist, sexist, classist, and ideological repression that exists in Cuba, preferring instead to openly support the regime. 

My friends and family urge me to draw on my reserves of mental and physical strength, hoping for a miracle. I for my part, feel that I am still the master of my future. There rises within me a rebellious spirit, that does not allow me to resign myself.

And despite abundant evidence and international recognition of the regime’s violations of international law regarding human rights, Cuba has a seat on the United Nations Human Rights Council, together with Iran. 

So here comes another end of the year, another New Year’s dinner in which we will be absent from the family table. 

What are we looking forward to in 2024? The Olympics? Díaz-Canel announces more misery and repression in the name of the eternal struggle of the regime against “the enemy.” Maybe he will even use the firing squad against us. Another Havana Biennial with a coterie of artists and intellectuals that participate as if nothing were happening in Cuba. With so many problems in the world, Cuba fades away, it does not even exist for most people. 

My friends and family urge me to draw on my reserves of mental and physical strength, hoping for a miracle. I for my part, feel that I am still the master of my future. There rises within me a rebellious spirit, that does not allow me to resign myself. I just hope to get through the depression and frustration that comes with the end of the year, surviving in these conditions. I will see what I can come up with to try to alter the reality around me in 2024.

This story was originally published in an article on WePresent by Alexander Durie. You can read the original article here.

Artist Hashim Nasr was on holiday in Egypt when civil war erupted at home in Sudan in April 2023. Forced to remain in Egypt for the foreseeable future and struggling to adapt, he threw himself into his art, creating his latest series “On War and Displacement.” He tells Alexander Durie how visualizing the emotional experience of exile helped him reckon with his situation, and how the series is an homage to those who remain on home soil.

When Hashim Nasr left Sudan with his family in early April 2023, he was initially just planning on spending Ramadan in Egypt, at his family’s holiday home near Alexandria. But two weeks later, civil war erupted in Sudan, as the paramilitary group the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) launched a full-scale attack on Khartoum in an attempt to take control of the country. “I packed only a small suitcase, not expecting to be away for long,” Nasr says. “It wasn’t a choice to stay in Egypt, but it was too dangerous to go back.”

I have this idea of longing for freedom.

Nasr is one of over 1.5 million Sudanese to have relocated to Egypt, as the war rages on in their country. Like many refugees, he struggled to adapt and feel at home in his new surroundings. In the first few months, he didn’t buy any furniture for his room and lived from his suitcase. “I just had this mentality that, at some point, I will go back to Sudan,” he says. What gave Nasr a sense of meaning and solace in this difficult period was his art. Specifically, developing a photo series on displacement—which he hoped Sudanese people in exile could relate to—in his characteristic style rooted in experimental and conceptual photography.

Take his image “Displacement North,” for instance, in which a model is on a rooftop in Alexandria, their face hidden by a large white cone, carrying a clock attached to a moon in one hand, and transporting a small suitcase tied to some birds in the other. The model in the shot is inspired by Nasr’s own feelings and experiences: “I have this idea of longing for freedom,” he says. “Birds always represent a longing for my personal home and freedom, carrying dreams and hopes with me, and the trauma of this war. The clock references the time when the war started—I had a phone call with my uncle at 7.20am on April 15 2023 when it started. And the suitcase has my own belongings.”

Nasr is timid and quiet, so even if much of his work explores the idea of the self, he doesn’t want to show his face or to be the center of attention. But sometimes, he says, art can be a form of resisting traditional ways of representing our identity. “The subjects are a way to hide my identity, and the models are my friends and neighbours,” he explains. “They don’t want to show their faces because they’re shy, and I wanted to give them a more secure space, so putting the cones on them gives them more confidence, and it’s a challenge for me to be more creative.”

While the series title, “On War and Displacement,” might invoke violent graphic images, perhaps of bloodied civilians, bombed hospitals or desperate refugees, Nasr’s photos are quite the opposite: colorful, vibrant and full of life, with a sense of magical realism, as if they were taken from a dream. “People need to engage more with different ways of documenting realities,” he says.

My way is maybe unfamiliar, but you have to question what photos are about—provoking this question has always been my purpose.

The project has received grants from the Prince Claus Fund, the Magnum Foundation and the Arab Fund for Arts and Culture (AFAC) as part of the prestigious Arab Documentary Photography Program. Another major step forward was being selected by The British Journal of Photography in its Ones to Watch in 2024. Nasr says that the first thing he did after receiving his grant was to buy his first professional camera. Before that, and still today, most of his images, including the ones from this series, are shot on his mobile phone, a Xiaomi Redmi Note 10 Pro. A big reason he continues to shoot with his phone is to avoid getting questioned by Egyptian authorities, who often stop people with big cameras and ask for permits.

Nasr finds inspiration for his images through real-life stories, and sometimes dreams. Every shot is first drawn by himself, before he buys the materials for them in markets, chooses a setting “related to surrealism, like the desert or the sea,” and then presents these drawings to his models. “I’m very perfectionist, [the photo] has to be exactly like my sketches,” he says.

Nasr’s longing for his family and his homesickness are felt deeply in this series. One photo, titled “The Safest Place was Under the Dining Table,” refers to a conversation he had with his aunt when she heard air strikes outside her home in Khartoum. Another shot, “Remembering My Uncle,” shows four male models, three with large blue cones over their faces, and one with a bouquet of flowers above his head. “We lost an uncle due to kidney failure in June 2023 because of a shortage of medicine [coming into Sudan],” Nasr says.

I have four uncles. He [the one who passed away] is the one with the flowers, to pay homage to his memories.

The mere act of sharing these images on his Instagram has provoked curiosity in people to learn more about what’s happening in Sudan, and the fate of Sudanese refugees scattered across the globe. This series, for him, is an “homage to those who are still in Sudan,” and evoke his “wish for the war to end as soon as possible.” “If I make just one person more interested in Sudan, I’m happy,” he says. “A [Sudanese] friend of mine told me that he feels connected with the characters in my photos as they tell his story. I couldn’t be more proud of that. It feels like I’m doing something meaningful.”

This story was originally published in an article on Made in China Journal by Bao Hongwei and Maghiel van Crevel. You can read the original article here.

Mu Cao, whose literary name means ‘grass on the graves’, is China’s first openly gay poet and his writing is ‘marked by a forcefulness that can sow the seeds of emancipation and social change’ (van Crevel 2024: 98).

He has been described as a ‘poet from among the common people’ and a ‘voice from the bottom of Chinese society’ (Words Without Borders 2016). The biographical details that accompany his work are at once ironic and serious. They are characterised more by what he is not and has not done than by what he is and has done: ‘He has no diplomas, he is not a member of the Chinese Writers Association, and he publishes almost entirely outside of official channels’ (Words Without Borders 2016). In one of his poetry collections, the inside cover notes tongue-in-cheek that he has ‘not yet won the Nobel Prize for Literature’ (Mu Cao 2002).

Mu Cao’s work is defined by its rootedness in unofficial, outside-the-system subalternity in Chinese society and its striking difference from mainstream literature. Both his queer sexuality and his decades-long experience as a precarious migrant worker put him at the margins of Chinese society. This double marginalisation has shaped the content and aesthetics of his creative work.

A Queer ‘Battler’ Poet

Mu Cao was born in 1974 into a rural household in Xihua County, Henan Province, one of the poorest regions in China. He dropped out of high school at age 15, following a conflict with his teacher. After helping his mother, a dressmaker, to run her makeshift street stall for a couple of years, he went to the provincial capital, Zhengzhou, to look for work. He thus joined the countless precarious internal migrant workers known in China as ‘battlers’ (打工者 or 打工人), meaning people who work for the boss, selling their labour because that is all they have, with no control over their destiny. The English translation used here comes from an Australian expression for lower-class people faced with similar economic insecurity who persevere in the face of adversity. It matches the linguistic register of the Chinese source term and, just like the latter, it can be either pejorative or worn as a badge of pride (van Crevel 2017b: 246; Wikipedia n.d.).

Since the 1980s, about 300 million people have left the Chinese countryside for the cities to seek economic betterment and urban adventure, and escape poverty and the strictures of village life. Having become fixtures in the Chinese cityscape wherever low-status work must be done (construction, cleaning, factory work, courier services, waste-picking, sex work, etcetera), they often generate unease or disdain among native urbanites and are structurally confronted with discrimination. Over the decades, first in Zhengzhou, then in Beijing, then in Zhengzhou again, Mu Cao has held a series of odd jobs—cleaner, cook, barber, street vendor, garage keeper, factory worker, and many more—none of which lasted long. He works to save enough money to quit so he can write, until the money runs out and he must find work again. Mu Cao has lived this precarious life, usually without a stable residence or medical insurance, for 35 years.

Mu Cao loves literature and his childhood dream was to become a writer. He taught himself poetry and fiction by reading whatever he could get his hands on, which meant an eclectic curriculum featuring many cheap pirated editions of Chinese and foreign classics. In 1998, he self-published his first poetry collection, titled Mu Cao’s Poetry (墓草的诗). He has since disowned it, dismissing his earliest work as immature lyricism. The real start of his creative career as a writer coincided with his discovery of his own gay sexuality. Around 2000, he discovered underground gay life in Zhengzhou and online. Soon after, he came out as gay in his poetry. The double marginalisation outlined above has underpinned his work ever since.

Despite being talented and writing diligently, Mu Cao found it difficult to get his work published, since both queerness and socioeconomic inequality count as politically sensitive topics in China. Having received numerous rejections from publishers and literary journals, Mu Cao was among the earliest literary authors to take to the internet to explore what came to be known as ‘web literature’ (网络文学). Under that umbrella, he worked tirelessly to advance ‘comrade literature’ (同志文学), with ‘comrade’ being an informal Chinese term to refer to LGBTQI+ people. In 2000, thanks to his web design skills (for which he had presciently taken a course in Zhengzhou), Mu Cao founded the ‘Comrade Poetry Web’ (同志诗歌网) and the ‘Comrade Poetry Forum’ (同志诗歌论坛), two websites that promoted queer Chinese-language poetry online. Later that year, he joined his fellow Henanese poet Ren Yu (人与, later known as Xiang Yu 向与) in establishing Scrutiny (审视), an unofficial poetry journal, and serving as its vice editor-in-chief. Mu Cao came out as gay in the first issue. The ‘Comrade Poetry Web’ was shut down in 2006, but Mu Cao continued showcasing his writing on his own website—designed in the colours of the rainbow flag—for many years, until this was also shut down, in the late 2010s (Mu Cao 2018).

Mu Cao’s contribution to queer literature has been recognised in the pages of GaySpot (乐点), China’s longest-running queer community magazine—also an unofficial publication. He served as co-editor of its first issue and the magazine has since championed his work. GaySpot anthologised his poetry in Islands (屿), a special issue on Chinese queer literature published in 2018. In 2022, the magazine also released an exquisitely crafted survey anthology of his poetry titled 20: Twenty Years of Mu Cao’s Poetry (20: 墓草20年诗选).

Mu Cao’s contribution to Chinese literature has largely been overlooked, perhaps due to the double stigmatisation of his sexuality and underclass status—and, of course, because censorship has rendered him close to invisible outside the official literary circuit. In fact, his talent and vision have long been in evidence, not just in his own writing but also in his work as an editor. In 2002, he edited an ambitious volume called the 2001 Chinese Web Poetry Yearbook (二〇〇一年度中国网络诗歌), which was intended as an annual publication but never made it past the first issue. In 2006, he served as editor of The Gaze: Twenty-First-Century Chinese Unofficial Avant-Garde Literature (凝望: 21世纪中国民间先锋文学). Both these books are headstrong, original publications that show an ambitious editorial vision and a determination to raise the visibility of contemporary Chinese writers whose styles ‘rock the boat’. In 2015, amid an ever-tightening political climate, Mu Cao was awarded the Underground Poetry Award by Freebooters (江湖), one of the most radical unofficial Chinese poetry journals in the new century.

如果全世界的警察和小偷
都这样！！！！！！！！！
天下不是太平了吗！

and even offered to find him a job

Mu Cao, whose literary name means ‘grass on the graves’, is China’s first openly gay poet and his writing is ‘marked by a forcefulness that can sow the seeds of emancipation and social change’ (van Crevel 2024: 98).

He has been described as a ‘poet from among the common people’ and a ‘voice from the bottom of Chinese society’ (Words Without Borders 2016). The biographical details that accompany his work are at once ironic and serious. They are characterised more by what he is not and has not done than by what he is and has done: ‘He has no diplomas, he is not a member of the Chinese Writers Association, and he publishes almost entirely outside of official channels’ (Words Without Borders 2016). In one of his poetry collections, the inside cover notes tongue-in-cheek that he has ‘not yet won the Nobel Prize for Literature’ (Mu Cao 2002).

Mu Cao’s work is defined by its rootedness in unofficial, outside-the-system subalternity in Chinese society and its striking difference from mainstream literature. Both his queer sexuality and his decades-long experience as a precarious migrant worker put him at the margins of Chinese society. This double marginalisation has shaped the content and aesthetics of his creative work.

A Queer ‘Battler’ Poet

Mu Cao was born in 1974 into a rural household in Xihua County, Henan Province, one of the poorest regions in China. He dropped out of high school at age 15, following a conflict with his teacher. After helping his mother, a dressmaker, to run her makeshift street stall for a couple of years, he went to the provincial capital, Zhengzhou, to look for work. He thus joined the countless precarious internal migrant workers known in China as ‘battlers’ (打工者 or 打工人), meaning people who work for the boss, selling their labour because that is all they have, with no control over their destiny. The English translation used here comes from an Australian expression for lower-class people faced with similar economic insecurity who persevere in the face of adversity. It matches the linguistic register of the Chinese source term and, just like the latter, it can be either pejorative or worn as a badge of pride (van Crevel 2017b: 246; Wikipedia n.d.).

items.content_html:
In a country where queer existence is often met with silence, repression, or outright hostility, art becomes both sanctuary and defiance. In this intimate and powerful interview, Georgian artist and 2023 Seed Awardee, Lucrezia, speaks with Val Dechev (Prince Claus Fund's Communications Coordinator) on reclaiming erased histories, using multidisciplinary art as a form of resistance, and the fragile hope of creating a future where queer lives are seen, remembered, and celebrated. Through performance, music, and photography, she challenges the systems that seek to erase them—and in doing so, build a world on their own terms.

For readers who may be unfamiliar with queer rights or the erasure of queer history in Georgia, could you briefly explain the context?

In Georgia, queer people exist in a paradox—always present, always erased. Our stories have been buried under silence, criminalisation, and shame, especially under Soviet rule and the conservative systems that followed. Today, visibility still comes with risk.

In recent years, we have witnessed a painful regression. Hard-won spaces of queer visibility are being violently shut down. The far right and state-aligned forces are working hand in hand to criminalize not just queer life, but even the memory of it. Drag is demonized, Pride is forbidden. The state no longer hides its disdain; it performs it. Many members of our community are forced to flee, exiled not just by violence, but by silence.

You've been exploring queer history as a source of power. How can reclaiming the past serve as queer resistance and resilience?

Queer art is rarely institutionally supported. It lives in the underground, where it’s vital but often invisible, underfunded, and undervalued.

The Seed Award gave me wings. It allowed me to experiment, to move beyond what I already knew, and to say more, to create more.

It reminded me that my voice isn’t just about surviving in the margins. It can take up space. It can build worlds.

Your performance work “Silver lining” evokes a statuesque but also religious imagery, while presenting your body as draped and nearly invisible. Can you tell us more about the piece and the choice for the draping?

Indeed, the piece plays with visibility and reverence. Draping became a metaphor for protection, for ritual, for absence. Invisibility, for queer people, is often survival. But in “Silver lining”, I turned it into a quiet superpower. A way to reclaim softness, holiness, and control over how I am seen.

The transparency in the piece speaks to queer visibility; how we are often seen through, but not truly seen. It was also an offering to all the queer people who don’t have the space or safety to speak out. Through this performance, I wanted to give voice to their silence. The poem embedded in the work was written as a kind of invocation; a wake-up call, a plea for people to see what has been made invisible. To feel the sacredness in queer existence.

I used traditional Georgian instruments and earth itself and soil as sound and presence. Earth is origin and memory. It connects the ritual to land, to ancestry, to the beginning of everything. Through that grounding, I tried to weave queerness back into a place it has always belonged to, even if it’s been denied.

What does the future look like to you?

Honestly, sometimes I’m scared of the future. I don’t know where I’ll be. I don’t know if I’ll still have space to create, to speak, to exist safely in the place I call home. Support has been cut. Repression is growing. Every day it feels like the walls are closing in a bit more for queer people in Georgia.

I try to hold on to hope, but it’s fragile.

Still, I believe in the invisible threads that bind us. I believe that even in exile, even in fear, we can carry the future with us in our bodies, in our art, in each other.

But lately, it feels like the future is slipping through our fingers. Like we are screaming into a void that has already made up its mind. And some days, I wonder if anyone is still listening.

items.content_html:
In a candid conversation with writer Lanre, Nigerian multidisciplinary artist Lady Donli, a 2024 Prince Claus Seed Awardee, reflects on her identity, vision, and purpose. Calling herself a “Pan-African rockstar”, Donli uses music, research, and curation to spotlight the African continent and challenge colonial legacies that fragment its identity. She traces her Pan-Africanism to personal heritage and lived experience, blending continental sounds to spark curiosity and connection. Speaking openly about the structural and gendered obstacles for creatives in Nigeria, she highlights her feminist activism, including founding the Yar’Uwa Sisterhood to support women in the arts. Her work combines resilience, pragmatism, and visionary thinking, from dreaming of functional African infrastructure to building sustainable pipelines for women behind the stage, embodying an active, lived Pan-Africanism.

Her hair is in knots, she looks fresh-faced and unbothered, but with a smile on her face. Here, I am staring, albeit through my camera lens into the eyes of the self-proclaimed “Pan-African rockstar.”  

This is Lady Donli: a multidisciplinary Nigerian artist and 2024 Seed Awardee whose work spans music, research, and curation. On the other side of the camera lens is me, Lanre, a writer and cultural accessibility researcher who shares her Nigerian heritage. The conversation starts with her describing her practice as grounded in a singular purpose. In her own words:

Whether it be via my music, or it could be via other people’s music that I work with, or it could be via archiving, or it could be, you know, via storytelling, but my main goal as an artist and as a creator is to spotlight the African continent in some way. 

This ambition to spotlight the African continent, and the notion of a Pan-African rockstar reveals itself not as a branding choice, but as a deliberate political claim. “I think being a Pan-African rock star is always giving credit to where the inspiration comes from,” she explains, a deliberate stance against a time when “being African wasn’t portrayed to be cool.” A goal of hers is offering others like her a language of cultural pride. For her, the title can almost be seen as some form of provocation, or even a portal inviting people to ask what it means, so she can respond with a story about a certain belonging that stretches beyond nationality and interrogates the very colonial borders carved onto the continent. This identity of hers is a political and cultural statement that actively redraws the map of the African continent, and it pushes beyond the borders imposed by European colonisers. She embodies this philosophy personally, identifying as both Hausa and Ijaw, two of the many Nigerian tribes, and even jokingly referring to herself as a “Pan-Nigerian”, before scaling it to a continental pride, to be loud about where she comes from, to be proud about it, and, unafraid to take up space. 

At this point, I am a bit curious, but mostly I feel it would be appropriate to help the reader understand what it means to be Pan African? Here, she breaks into a slight chuckle, almost a laugh even... And starts out reciting a Marcus Garvey quote,

“A people without knowledge of their past history, origin and culture is like a tree without roots”.

For her, this philosophy translates to an all-encompassing identity that supersedes the arbitrary borders of nations. She illustrates this with her own family’s history, tracing her roots to present day Chad before her great grandfather acclimatised in Nigeria, a personal story that highlights the continent’s deep, intertwined connections. This perspective is re-affirmed in her daily life, where she finds linguistic and often melodic similarities across the continent from Ivorian rhythms to Ghanaian high-life and Congolese guitar; all revealing the artificiality of colonial divisions. For her, Pan-Africanism is this lived reality, a conscious choice to see the fickle nature of these borders and to champion a unified, rooted, and representative African continent above all else. 

So, what is the role of music in this Pan-African vision? For Donli, as she preferred to be called, it is the essential thread that weaves the ideology into a lived experience. She deliberately blends sounds from across the continent to function as a gateway, that is designed ‘not’ to lecture, but to spark a chain reaction of curiosity. A listener might hear a familiar pattern and be sent on a quest, searching for the Ivorian artist from whomst it originated, which might then lead them to explore Ivorian cuisine, and ultimately, to a conversation with someone from that culture where they discover shared similarities. And, her music as a starting point, a deliberate catalyst meant to dissolve borders by encouraging people to “think a bit more deeply”, transforming the abstract Pan-Africanism into a tangible, personal journey of connection and or discovery that allows people to dig beneath the surface of the music. 

I proceed to ask her to dream up a theoretical Pan-African future for either the continent or even Nigeria as a country. She starts out with a disclaimer, promising to disappoint me with her response. We both chuckle here, I have an inclination of the direction she is heading to with her next words. There would be no visions of flying cars or abstract utopias. Her dream, forged and firmly situated in the daily grind of Lagos, is profoundly simple: “I just want a functional country.” She paints a picture of a foundational paradise: roads without potholes, reliable healthcare, constant electricity, and accessible internet; where productivity and learning aren’t luxuries. This vision immediately expands from Nigeria to the entire continent, noting that the story of infrastructural failure is a tragically unifying African narrative. “I want an Africa that works,” she states, where the ability to meet basic human needs isn’t determined by one’s status. For an artist whose entire ethos is about celebrating and touring Africa, this dream is the ultimate enabler. The freedom she truly seeks is the ability to build a life and a career entirely on her own terms, and, on her own continent. 

We delve into what these challenges mean for her as an artist, for her creativity. The answer is a sobering lesson in some very practical logistics. Her Pan-African vision is perpetually hampered by a need for external validation and capital. “I can’t sustain myself in Nigeria, or on the African continent alone... I have to go to other spaces and look for funding,” she states, revealing that even our conversation is facilitated by a foreign grant. This relentless outward search stunts her growth, a stark contrast to the organic ecosystems she observes for artists abroad where, the ladder of progression is clear: small venues lead to larger ones. In Nigeria, she explains, a performer must be their own entire production company, scouting the space, building the stage, and sourcing sound and light, all with unreliable equipment. This DIY reality doesn’t just strain resources; it corrodes the very confidence required to dream big. Her conclusion is devastatingly simple: “Nigeria is a place where dreams come to die.” At this point in our conversation, we sigh. It takes us a minute to gain some re-composure to continue the interview, a certain sense of despair fills me, and a somewhat overwhelming sadness. 

However, my curiosity is piqued about how she navigates all of these compounding issues particularly as a woman in the industry. She meets the question with a weary clarity. “Nigeria can be a misogynistic place, but not unlike anywhere else in the world to be honest”, she states, explaining that the struggle is especially acute for a woman with a world-view of what life could be. Her strategy is one of unwavering principle and community. Navigating it, for her, means being “really strong in my politics, you know, my feminist politics,” and channelling that into tangible action. This isn’t just about personal survival; it’s about building a new ecosystem. She has founded a community called the “Yar’Uwa sisterhood,” a safe space that offers workshops and advice for creative women, a kind of concrete effort to create the support system the industry lacks. Her mantra is to block out the noise and focus on her vision of a more equitable music scene in Nigeria, and the continent at large. 

Her vision is defiantly collective. “I don’t care to be the first woman to do anything,” she explains, rejecting the lonely pinnacle of being a symbolic “first.” Instead, her goal is to create a “revolving door” of opportunity, ensuring that when one woman enters a space, she holds it open for others. This philosophy demands action, leading her to ask uncomfortable questions, as she did when finding herself as the only woman in a campaign photo-shoot and challenging the organisers’ patronising label of “strong.” Such insistence often leads to her being perceived as a “diva” or a “bad guy”. Labels she has learned to embrace, understanding them simply as the price for being a woman who advocates for herself and others. 

This steadfast commitment to her politics inevitably invites blowback, but she meets it with a kind of serene defiance. When asked if she is afraid of pushbacks, she responds:

You see that I fought for a cause, I fought for marginalised people, and that’s all that matters to me.

She traces this conviction to a journey that began when she first identified as a feminist at 17, despite her initial fear of the label. Now, over a decade later, that fear has transformed into a source of strength. This sentiment is the very embodiment of resilience. When I ask her to define what that word “resilience” truly means for her as an African creative, the question prompts a knowing chuckle from us both. Our chuckling is absurd in the context of such a heavy topic, yet perhaps that is the point. For Donli, resilience is not an abstract virtue but a daily, grinding necessity. “The reason I’m consistently saying resilience is because we are given so little,” she explains, describing the compounded barriers of being a woman in Nigeria and a Black woman abroad as “blocks on blocks on blocks on blocks.”. 

Her resilience, therefore, is this conscious focus on a distant horizon; spreading Pan-Africanism through music and creating that “revolving door” for women. It is what allows her to endure the constant fight for visibility and against being forgotten. “Every day you’re just fighting for something,” she says, framing it as an active, daily struggle to not only secure her own place but to carve out a space so visible it becomes a beacon, ensuring her story becomes a roadmap for others. 

The conversation turns to her recent recognition as a Prince Claus Seed Awardee. When asked what the award means for her art, she dons a pageant-winner’s smile, describing it as a “vital framework for dreaming.” For an artist working in an environment that often stifles dreams, this was transformative. “It felt like someone had taken their foot off my head,” she says, the relief palpable in her voice. That breath of air allowed her to move from ideation to action, specifically to launch the women’s program, the Yar’Uwa Sisterhood, which she had long envisioned but lacked the resources to start. 

This financial support has become a channel for exploring the fuller spectrum of her creativity. It allowed her to begin work on her first-ever sound installation, a product of the research her archiving mind loves. More than just funding a project, it empowered a purpose of extending her creative practice beyond personal gain to actively empower her community. The fund also provided an unexpected bonus: an extended community. Through it, she connected with fellow Prince Claus Award recipients who have since become both collaborators and friends, proving that the Award’s value wasn’t just monetary, but also about building a network of allies for the long haul. 

I want to probe a bit more, curious to know what hid behind this pageant answer, asking for a more critical, perhaps even a de-colonial perspective. At this point, we go off the record and decide to keep it at that. However, as a skillful negotiator that I am, I manage to negotiate some details on the record. She articulates the central dilemma with a clear-eyed precision. She acknowledges the exploitative potential of these systems, noting how some foreign entities are “extractive without adding much value to the local ecosystem.” Yet, she immediately pivots to a haunting, open-ended question: if you take away these funds, “where does that leave a lot of African creatives?” For an artist trying to do meaningful research or build a sustainable career, the options are vanishingly few. With local infrastructure and independent labels struggling, her conclusion was a sobering piece of pragmatism. For now, she sees external funding as somewhat necessary, if imperfect, a means to an end; the essential ability to “bring back more into the country and continent.” 

As we are now rounding up the interview, I proceed to ask her to dream; if she could get an even bigger fund, how would she channel those resources? The answer is immediate and precise, a vision that stretches from her community to the continent. She spoke of transforming her safe space for women (Yar’Uwa sisterhood) into a full-fledged residency program, building a pan-African network where creative women could connect and explore their art with unwavering support. But her dream drills down to a specific, critical deficit; the lack of women behind the stage.

We don’t have light technicians that are women. We don’t have a lot of stage designers that are women. We don’t have a lot of sound engineers.

Her goal isn’t just a one-off workshop, but years of sustained mentorship and access, creating a system where a female performer can finally work with a female technician who intuitively understands her vision. It is a dream of profound, structural change, one where the backstage crew finally reflects the woman on the stage.  

Her hair still in knots, her face still fresh and with that same unbothered smile, she thanks me. Altogether, I leave our conversation feeling like, these indeed are the markings of a true Pan-African rockstar.

She meets the question with a weary clarity. “Nigeria can be a misogynistic place, but not unlike anywhere else in the world to be honest”, she states, explaining that the struggle is especially acute for a woman with a world-view of what life could be. Her strategy is one of unwavering principle and community. Navigating it, for her, means being “really strong in my politics, you know, my feminist politics,” and channelling that into tangible action. This isn’t just about personal survival; it’s about building a new ecosystem. She has founded a community called the “Yar’Uwa sisterhood,” a safe space that offers workshops and advice for creative women, a kind of concrete effort to create the support system the industry lacks. Her mantra is to block out the noise and focus on her vision of a more equitable music scene in Nigeria, and the continent at large. 

Her vision is defiantly collective. “I don’t care to be the first woman to do anything,” she explains, rejecting the lonely pinnacle of being a symbolic “first.” Instead, her goal is to create a “revolving door” of opportunity, ensuring that when one woman enters a space, she holds it open for others. This philosophy demands action, leading her to ask uncomfortable questions, as she did when finding herself as the only woman in a campaign photo-shoot and challenging the organisers’ patronising label of “strong.” Such insistence often leads to her being perceived as a “diva” or a “bad guy”. Labels she has learned to embrace, understanding them simply as the price for being a woman who advocates for herself and others. 

This steadfast commitment to her politics inevitably invites blowback, but she meets it with a kind of serene defiance. When asked if she is afraid of pushbacks, she responds:

You see that I fought for a cause, I fought for marginalised people, and that’s all that matters to me.

She traces this conviction to a journey that began when she first identified as a feminist at 17, despite her initial fear of the label. Now, over a decade later, that fear has transformed into a source of strength. This sentiment is the very embodiment of resilience. When I ask her to define what that word “resilience” truly means for her as an African creative, the question prompts a knowing chuckle from us both. Our chuckling is absurd in the context of such a heavy topic, yet perhaps that is the point. For Donli, resilience is not an abstract virtue but a daily, grinding necessity. “The reason I’m consistently saying resilience is because we are given so little,” she explains, describing the compounded barriers of being a woman in Nigeria and a Black woman abroad as “blocks on blocks on blocks on blocks.”. 

Her resilience, therefore, is this conscious focus on a distant horizon; spreading Pan-Africanism through music and creating that “revolving door” for women. It is what allows her to endure the constant fight for visibility and against being forgotten. “Every day you’re just fighting for something,” she says, framing it as an active, daily struggle to not only secure her own place but to carve out a space so visible it becomes a beacon, ensuring her story becomes a roadmap for others. 

The conversation turns to her recent recognition as a Prince Claus Seed Awardee. When asked what the award means for her art, she dons a pageant-winner’s smile, describing it as a “vital framework for dreaming.” For an artist working in an environment that often stifles dreams, this was transformative. “It felt like someone had taken their foot off my head,” she says, the relief palpable in her voice. That breath of air allowed her to move from ideation to action, specifically to launch the women’s program, the Yar’Uwa Sisterhood, which she had long envisioned but lacked the resources to start. 

This financial support has become a channel for exploring the fuller spectrum of her creativity. It allowed her to begin work on her first-ever sound installation, a product of the research her archiving mind loves. More than just funding a project, it empowered a purpose of extending her creative practice beyond personal gain to actively empower her community. The fund also provided an unexpected bonus: an extended community. Through it, she connected with fellow Prince Claus Award recipients who have since become both collaborators and friends, proving that the Award’s value wasn’t just monetary, but also about building a network of allies for the long haul. 

I want to probe a bit more, curious to know what hid behind this pageant answer, asking for a more critical, perhaps even a de-colonial perspective. At this point, we go off the record and decide to keep it at that. However, as a skillful negotiator that I am, I manage to negotiate some details on the record. She articulates the central dilemma with a clear-eyed precision. She acknowledges the exploitative potential of these systems, noting how some foreign entities are “extractive without adding much value to the local ecosystem.” Yet, she immediately pivots to a haunting, open-ended question: if you take away these funds, “where does that leave a lot of African creatives?” For an artist trying to do meaningful research or build a sustainable career, the options are vanishingly few. With local infrastructure and independent labels struggling, her conclusion was a sobering piece of pragmatism. For now, she sees external funding as somewhat necessary, if imperfect, a means to an end; the essential ability to “bring back more into the country and continent.” 

As we are now rounding up the interview, I proceed to ask her to dream; if she could get an even bigger fund, how would she channel those resources? The answer is immediate and precise, a vision that stretches from her community to the continent. She spoke of transforming her safe space for women (Yar’Uwa sisterhood) into a full-fledged residency program, building a pan-African network where creative women could connect and explore their art with unwavering support. But her dream drills down to a specific, critical deficit; the lack of women behind the stage.

We don’t have light technicians that are women. We don’t have a lot of stage designers that are women. We don’t have a lot of sound engineers.

Her goal isn’t just a one-off workshop, but years of sustained mentorship and access, creating a system where a female performer can finally work with a female technician who intuitively understands her vision. It is a dream of profound, structural change, one where the backstage crew finally reflects the woman on the stage.  

Her hair still in knots, her face still fresh and with that same unbothered smile, she thanks me. Altogether, I leave our conversation feeling like, these indeed are the markings of a true Pan-African rockstar.

Kim Schuiten werkt sinds kort als projectmedewerker bij Stichting Democratie en Media. Ze studeerde politicologie aan de Universiteit van Amsterdam en was werkzaam voor onder meer Amnesty International. ‘Veel mensen hebben al moeite om hun boodschappen te betalen, laat staan een krantenabonnement erbij nemen.’

Wat trekt jou aan in het werkveld van Stichting Democratie en Media?
‘Ik ben altijd al politiek en maatschappelijk betrokken geweest. De afgelopen jaren zie ik hoe kwetsbaar ons medialandschap eigenlijk is. Het werkveld van SDM trekt me aan omdat het op het snijvlak zit van media, democratie en technologie. Precies de plek waar ik denk dat het verschil gemaakt kan worden én ik me hierin kan verdiepen.’

Hoe uitte die betrokkenheid zich in het verleden?
‘Ik heb me veel geïnteresseerd in ongelijkheidsvraagstukken, in mijn studietijd al. Welke mensen en welke landen vergaren geld en macht? En ten koste van wie en wat gebeurt dat? Na mijn studie ben ik gaan werken in de cultuursector, waar die vragen spelen in het klein: wie heeft de macht om te bepalen wat er in een museum hangt? In mijn tijd bij Amnesty International heb ik me met verschillende maatschappelijke thema’s beziggehouden, maar altijd vanuit het streven naar gelijkheid.’

Doen die ongelijkheidsvraagstukken zich ook voort in het vakgebied van SDM?
‘Absoluut! Ik heb bijvoorbeeld best veel publieksprogramma’s bijgewoond over directe democratie [een bestuursvorm waarin burgers direct invloed hebben op wetgeving en beleid, SDM]. Het waren altijd dezelfde mensen die daarop afkwamen; veelal witte, hoogopgeleide mensen die hun weg al goed weten te vinden in ons ingewikkelde democratische stelsel. Zo werkt een democratie wat mij betreft precies niet. Hoe zorgen we ervoor dat alle mensen betrokken kunnen en willen blijven? Relevant, zeker nu het vertrouwen in de democratie daalt.

Gelijkheid gaat ook over gelijke toegang tot betrouwbare informatie; kennis is macht. Als niet iedereen dezelfde informatie kán krijgen, ontstaat er een disbalans in de machtsverhoudingen tussen burgers mét en burgers zonder kennis. Ik maak me zorgen over of mensen die minder goed geïnformeerd zijn, ook makkelijker kunnen worden gemanipuleerd en vatbaarder zijn voor populisme en de waan van de dag.

Wat is hierin de rol van journalistiek?
‘Veel mensen scrollen tegenwoordig op Instagram en TikTok in plaats van nieuwswebsites. Toen ik net was afgestudeerd heb ik mijn krantenabonnement opgezegd omdat het gewoon te duur voor me werd. Ik snap het heel goed dat veel mensen zeggen: “Ik heb moeite om mijn boodschappen te betalen aan het einde van de maand. Ik lees het nieuws wel online.”

Alleen worden we op sociale media voortdurend murw geslagen door informatie die inspeelt op onze gevoelens maar niet per se waar is. Daarom is het goed dat een platform als NOS Stories zoveel jongeren informeert. Er mag meer gedegen journalistiek in onze feed voorbijkomen.’

Bij SDM ben je aan de slag gegaan als projectmedewerker. Wat houdt dat in?
‘Hoewel ik een hekel heb aan de term “spin in het web”, is dat wel mijn functie. Ik ben betrokken bij alle projecten die we doen en help waar mogelijk. Van veel dingen weet ik wel een beetje, maar ik heb niet de diepe expertise op een onderwerp zoals sommige collega’s hier hebben. Het is mijn taak om met ze mee te denken en het project te laten slagen.’

SDM is een stuk kleiner dan je vorige werkgever, hoe is dat?
‘Kleine ideële organisaties zijn niet altijd even professioneel georganiseerd, waardoor ze wel goede ideeën hebben maar de slagkracht missen om écht impact te creëren. Grote organisaties als Amnesty missen soms de snelheid om snel te reageren op actualiteit. Toen ik binnenkwam bij SDM verbaasde het mij hoe goed alles hier geregeld is, maar ook hoe dynamisch er wordt samengewerkt. Het team is goed op elkaar ingespeeld en vertrouwt elkaar. De organisatie is open en supportive, maar blijft ook scherp en kritisch als het moet.’

delen:

Het bericht Ontmoet Kim Schuiten, onze nieuwe projectmedewerker verscheen eerst op Stichting Democratie en Media.
